How can a computer store something we hear and see?
units.text:
Encoding Sound and Video
How can a computer store something we hear and see?

units.label: slide 2
units.text:
Sound Is Analog
Real sound is a continuous wave.
Air pressure continuously changes
A microphone converts these changes into an electrical signal
computers cannot directly store an infinite continuous signal
How can we turn this wave into numbers?

units.label: slide 3
units.text:
Sampling
Sampling = measuring the signal repeatedly
Instead of remembering the entire continuous wave:
We measure its value many times every second.
Each measurement = sample

units.label: slide 4
units.text:
Sampling – Sample Rate
How often do we take a sample?
Sample rate = number of samples per second (Hz)
48 kHz = 48 000 samples/s
What happens if we take too few samples?

units.label: slide 5
units.text:
More Samples = Better Representation
Higher sample rate → the digital version follows the original wave more closely.
But:
Higher sample rate → more data.

Quality vs Size trade-off.

units.label: slide 6
units.text:
But What Number Do We Store?
Sampling tells us when we measure.
Now we need to describe how accurately we store each measurement.
Bit depth

8 bits → 256 possible levels
16 bits → 65,536 possible levels

More bits → more possible values → more accurate.

units.label: slide 7
units.text:
Sample Rate vs Bit Depth
Sample rate
How often do we measure?
Bit depth
How precisely do we measure?


Both increase quality — and both increase the amount of data.

units.label: slide 8
units.text:
Mono vs Stereo
Mono - 1 audio channel
Stereo - 2 audio channels
Left
Right

Stereo needs roughly twice as much raw audio data as mono.

units.label: slide 9
units.text:
How Much Data Does Sound Need?
Formula: sample rate × bit depth × channels = bits per second

For 48 kHz and 16 bit depth:
48,000 samples/s × 16 bits × 2 channels = 1,536,000 bits/s 

1,536,000 ÷ 8 = 192,000 bytes/s

So one second of uncompressed audio is about 192 kB

3 min song → 192kB ×180 = 34 560 kB = 34 MB

units.label: slide 10
units.text:
Uncompressed (Stores the audio without compression)
Example: 
	WAV
Lossless (No original information is lost)
Example:
	FLAC
Lossy (Some information is removed)
Examples:
	MP3, AAC

|Uncompressed| > |lossless| >  |lossy|
Audio Compression

units.label: slide 11
units.text:
Psychoacoustic Compression
JPEG uses limitations of our eyes (last lesson).

Audio compression can use limitations of our ears.
Examples of the idea:
very quiet sounds can be hidden by louder sounds
some frequencies are harder for us to hear
less noticeable information can be stored less accurately or removed
MP3 tries to remove information that we are unlikely to notice.

units.label: slide 12
units.text:
Recording:
Sound → Microphone → A/D converter → Digital data
A/D: Analog → Digital

Playback
Digital data → D/A converter → Speaker → Sound
D/A: Digital → Analog
A/D and D/A

units.label: slide 13
units.ocr_text:
What Is Video?

What does FPS stand for?
units.text:
What Is Video?

What does FPS stand for?

units.label: slide 14
units.text:
Video
Video = a sequence of images shown very quickly + audio

FPS = Frames Per Second
Examples:
24 FPS (cinema/movies)
30 FPS
60 FPS
Slow motion: Record at a high FPS, then play the video back at a lower FPS.

units.label: slide 15
units.text:
What Does 1080p Mean (on YouTube)?
When we choose 1080p, the number usually tells us the vertical resolution:
1080p = 1080 rows of pixels
The number of columns depends on the aspect ratio of the video.
So: 1080p does not always mean exactly 1920 × 1080.
Aspect ratio	Resolution
16:9	1920 × 1080
4:3	1440 × 1080

units.label: slide 16
units.text:
Why might we want more/less FPS?
What is the disadvantage of using more FPS?
Would every type of video benefit from 120 FPS?
Why might a football match benefit more from 60 FPS than a normal movie?

units.label: slide 17
units.text:
How big would raw video be (1 min, 30 FPS, Full HD)?
Full HD RGB image ≈ 6 MB
30 FPS:
6 MB × 30 ≈ 180 MB every second
One minute: ≈ 10–11 GB

And that is only Full HD and only 1 minute.
Imagine 4K, 3 hour movie.

units.label: slide 18
units.text:
How Can We Compress Video?
Two basic ideas:

1. Compress each frame
Similar to compressing an image.

2. Do not store everything again
Consecutive frames are often very similar.

units.label: slide 19
units.text:
Keyframes and Changes
Frame 1 — full imageFrame 2 — only changesFrame 3 — only changesFrame 4 — only changes
……

new full frame

A keyframe stores a complete image. Other frames can often be described using changes from nearby frames.

units.label: slide 20
units.text:
Codec vs Container
Codec = How the video/audio is compressed and encoded
Examples:
H.264, H.265, AV1

Container = A file that can contain:
Video, audio, subtitles, metadata
Examples:
MP4, MKV

MP4 is a container - H.264 is the codec inside it.

units.label: slide 21
units.text:
Four main things:

Resolution (HD, Full HD, 4K, …)
FPS (24 FPS, 30 FPS, 60 FPS, …)
Bitrate (How much data is used every second)
Compression / Codec (How efficiently the data is stored)
What Affects Video File Size?

units.label: slide 22
units.text:
Video Bitrate (Mbit/s)
With raw video, the amount of data is mainly determined by the raw frames themselves.
With compressed video, the encoder has to decide how much data it can use to describe each second.
Bitrate = the data „budget“ for each second of compressed video
If the bitrate is too low, the codec has to throw away more information, which can cause:
blur
blocky areas
loss of fine detail
Higher bitrate = more data available to preserve image quality.
